why.correct: The plexus formed by the ventral rami of C5 to T1, at the level of the shoulder, is the brachial plexus. Its nerves supply the upper limb.
options: The cervical plexus is higher, formed by C1 to C4. It supplies the neck and the diaphragm, not the arm.
Correct. C5 to T1 form the brachial plexus.
The lumbar plexus comes from L1 to L4 in the lower back and supplies the front of the thigh.
The sacral plexus sits in the pelvis, from L4 to S4, and supplies the back of the thigh, the leg and the foot.

why.correct: The phrenic nerve leaves the cervical plexus (C3 to C5) and runs down to the diaphragm, its only motor supply.
options: The axillary nerve leaves the brachial plexus toward the shoulder and deltoid, not down to the diaphragm.
Intercostal nerves are thoracic ventral rami running between the ribs. They do not come from the cervical plexus.
Correct. This is the phrenic nerve, from C3 to C5.
The ulnar nerve comes from the lower brachial plexus (C8 and T1) and runs to the hand.

why.correct: The sciatic nerve is the thick nerve leaving the sacral plexus for the back of the thigh. It is the largest nerve in the body and later divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves.
options: The femoral nerve leaves the lumbar plexus for the front of the thigh.
Correct. The thick nerve from the sacral plexus is the sciatic nerve.
The obturator nerve leaves the lumbar plexus through the obturator foramen to the medial thigh; it is much thinner.
The tibial nerve is one of the two branches the sciatic nerve divides into, lower down, not the whole trunk.

why.correct: The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the brachial plexus that runs to the back of the arm and forearm and supplies the extensors.
options: The median nerve runs down the middle of the front of the forearm to the carpal tunnel. On this figure it is the branch just above the pinned one.
The ulnar nerve is the lowest of this group on the figure, the one heading to the medial side of the forearm and hand.
Correct. This is the radial nerve.
The axillary nerve is the highest branch shown, turning toward the shoulder.

why.correct: The femoral nerve (L2 to L4) leaves the lumbar plexus, passes into the front of the thigh and supplies the quadriceps femoris.
options: Correct. This is the femoral nerve.
The common fibular nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve behind the knee, far lower than this.
The sciatic nerve runs down the back of the thigh from the sacral plexus, not across the front.
The obturator nerve also comes from L2 to L4, but on this figure it is the branch just below the pinned one, heading to the medial thigh.

why.correct: You have 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal. There are 8 cervical nerves but only 7 cervical vertebrae, because C1 leaves above the first vertebra.
options: The total is right, but there are 8 cervical nerves, not 7, and only 1 coccygeal.
Nerves do not match vertebrae one for one: there is an extra cervical nerve, and the fused sacral and coccygeal bones give 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal nerve.
Correct. 8 + 12 + 5 + 5 + 1 = 31 pairs.
Twelve pairs is the count of thoracic spinal nerves only; they are one part of the full 31.

why.correct: The epineurium wraps the whole nerve, the perineurium wraps each fascicle inside it, and the endoneurium wraps each single axon.
options: Outermost: dense irregular connective tissue around the whole nerve.
Around each fascicle, a bundle of axons.
Around each single axon and its Schwann cells.
The axon itself is the innermost part.

why.correct: Each bundle is a fascicle, and the perineurium wraps each fascicle. Its cells are joined by tight junctions and control what passes from the blood into the fascicle.
options: The epineurium wraps the whole nerve and holds the fascicles together; it is the outer layer, not the sleeve around each bundle.
The endoneurium wraps single axons inside a fascicle, not whole bundles.
Correct. The perineurium wraps each fascicle.
Myelin wraps single axons and is made by Schwann cells; it is not a connective tissue layer around a bundle.

why.correct: The dorsal root is purely sensory, so cutting it removes input from its dermatome, reduced rather than abolished because of overlap, while every motor pathway through the ventral root is spared.

variables.name: Action potentials reaching the L5 dorsal horn from the L5 dermatome
variables.why: The sensory axons from the L5 dermatome enter the cord only through the L5 dorsal root, which is cut.

variables.name: Sensation over the top of the right foot (L5 dermatome)
variables.why: L5 signals no longer arrive, so sensation falls. It is reduced rather than absent, because the L4 and S1 dermatomes overlap this area.

variables.name: Motor commands leaving the cord through the L5 ventral root
variables.why: The motor axons leave through the ventral root, which is intact, so the brain can still send commands out.

variables.name: Strength of ankle dorsiflexion when the person tries
variables.why: The motor axons to the dorsiflexors are uncut, so voluntary strength is kept.

why.correct: The radial nerve spirals around the shaft of the humerus and supplies the wrist and finger extensors. Damage there causes wrist drop.
options: The median nerve supplies most of the flexors of the wrist and fingers and the thenar muscles. Damage weakens gripping and the thumb, not extension.
Correct. Wrist drop after a mid-shaft humerus fracture points to the radial nerve.
The ulnar nerve supplies most of the small muscles inside the hand. Damage weakens finger spreading and can curl the ring and little fingers, but wrist extension is spared.
The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the elbow flexors at the front of the arm, not the wrist extensors.

why.correct: The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel and supplies the skin of the thumb, index and middle fingers on the palm side and most of the thenar muscles. Squeezing it there is carpal tunnel syndrome.
options: The ulnar nerve supplies the little finger and half the ring finger, which feel normal here.
The radial nerve supplies the extensors and mainly the back of the hand; it does not explain numb fingertips on the palm side with a weak pinch.
The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and the skin over the shoulder, far from the fingers.
Correct. This is the median nerve, compressed in the carpal tunnel.

why.correct: The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, just under the skin. It carries sensation from the little finger and half the ring finger, so a knock there tingles in those fingers.
options: The radial nerve runs on the back and outer side of the arm; its skin area is the back of the hand near the thumb, not the little finger.
Correct. The "funny bone" is the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.
The median nerve supplies the thumb side of the palm and fingers, not the little finger.
The axillary nerve supplies the shoulder, not the hand.

why.correct: The common fibular nerve wraps around the neck of the fibula just under the skin and supplies the dorsiflexors at the front of the leg. Damage causes foot drop.
options: The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps; damage makes the knee buckle, not the toes drag.
The tibial nerve runs deep in the back of the leg to the plantar flexors, so it is not easily hit at the side of the knee, and its loss would weaken pushing off rather than lifting the foot.
The obturator nerve supplies the adductors of the medial thigh, not the muscles that lift the foot.
Correct. A blow at the fibular neck injures the common fibular nerve, causing foot drop.

why.correct: The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) is the diaphragm’s only motor supply. A C7 injury leaves those segments connected to the brain, so the diaphragm still contracts. Everything below it loses control from the brain, including the hand segments (C8 and T1), the trunk and the legs.
options: A C2 injury is above C3, so it cuts every phrenic nerve segment off from the brain. The diaphragm would stop and he would need a ventilator.
Correct. C3 to C5 are spared, so the phrenic nerves still drive the diaphragm, but the hands, trunk and legs lose control.
A T6 injury is below the hand segments (C8 and T1), so his grip would still work.
An L1 injury spares the hands and most of the trunk; only the legs and lower body would be affected.

why.correct: Both rami are mixed. The dorsal ramus supplies the back. The ventral ramus supplies the front and sides of the trunk and the limbs, forming the plexuses in the neck and limb regions and the intercostal nerves in the thorax.
options: Correct. The dorsal ramus turns backward to the erector spinae and the skin near the midline of the back.
Correct. The limbs are supplied by ventral rami, through the brachial, lumbar and sacral plexuses.
Incorrect. Rami form after the dorsal and ventral roots have joined, so each carries both sensory and motor axons.
Correct. T1 to T11 ventral rami run alone between the ribs as intercostal nerves.
Incorrect. All the plexuses, the brachial included, are formed from ventral rami.

why.correct: Each of the three trunks splits into an anterior and a posterior division, and the divisions regroup into the lateral, posterior and medial cords.
options: The roots of the brachial plexus are themselves ventral rami; rami come before the trunks, not after.
Correct. Trunks split into divisions, which regroup into cords.
Fascicles are bundles of axons inside any nerve, not a stage of the plexus.
Ganglia are clusters of cell bodies. The plexus holds only axons.

why.correct: The navel lies in the T10 dermatome. The thoracic dermatomes run as horizontal bands, T4 at the nipple line and T10 at the navel.
options: T4 is the nipple line, marker 5, well above the navel.
Correct. The navel is the T10 landmark.
L1 supplies the groin, marker 7, below the navel.
T12 lies below the navel, just above the groin.

why.correct: The thumb is in the C6 dermatome. Across the hand, C6 is the thumb, C7 the middle finger and C8 the little finger.
options: C5 supplies the outer side of the upper arm, marker 1, not the thumb.
C8 supplies the little finger side of the hand, marker 4.
C7 supplies the middle finger, marker 3.
Correct. The thumb is the C6 landmark.

why.correct: The outer edge of the foot, the little toe and the heel form the S1 dermatome, so the S1 root is the likely one.
options: L4 supplies the inner side of the leg below the knee, marker 8.
L5 supplies the top of the foot and the big toe, marker 9.
Correct. The lateral foot and little toe are the S1 landmark.
S3 supplies skin near the buttocks and perineum, not the foot.

why.correct: Each patch of skin is supplied mainly by one spinal nerve and partly by the ones above and below. With only T8 cut, T7 and T9 still carry some signals from the band, so sensation is reduced but not lost.
options: Correct. Overlap from neighboring dermatomes keeps partial sensation.
The ventral root carries motor axons out; it cannot bring sensory signals in to replace a cut dorsal root.
The ganglion holds the cell bodies, but their central axons run through the cut root to the cord, so the ganglion alone cannot deliver the signal.
Regrowth, where it happens, takes weeks to months at about a millimeter a day, and cut dorsal roots regrow into the cord poorly.

why.correct: After chickenpox the virus stays dormant in the sensory cell bodies of a dorsal root ganglion. When it reactivates it travels out along those axons, so the rash fills that ganglion’s dermatome on one side: here T10, which reaches the navel.
options: Correct. The right T10 dorsal root ganglion holds the sensory cell bodies for that band.
The ventral horn holds motor neurons. A reactivation there would not produce a rash following one sensory strip of skin.
The rash appears in the skin, but the virus waits between outbreaks inside nerve cell bodies, not in the skin.
The ventral root carries motor axons and holds no cell bodies.

why.correct: The sole is supplied by the tibial nerve, which joins the sciatic nerve and runs up the back of the thigh into the sacral plexus. The femoral nerve belongs to the lumbar plexus and serves the front of the thigh, so it is not on this path.
options: Correct step. The signal starts at a sensory ending in the skin of the sole.
Correct step. The tibial nerve supplies the sole of the foot.
Correct step. The tibial nerve is one of the two branches that make up the sciatic nerve.
This is the wrong step. The femoral nerve runs down the front of the thigh from the lumbar plexus; it plays no part in this path.
Correct step. The sciatic nerve comes from the sacral plexus, whose axons sort back into ventral rami and spinal nerves.
Correct step. In the spinal nerve, sensory axons pass their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion and enter the cord through the dorsal root.

why.correct: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus and supplies the deltoid, the main abductor of the arm, and the skin over the shoulder.
options: The radial nerve is at risk lower on the humerus, around its shaft, and its loss causes wrist drop rather than a weak shoulder.
Correct. The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and wraps the surgical neck.
The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the elbow flexors, not the deltoid.
The phrenic nerve runs to the diaphragm, not to the shoulder muscles.

why.correct: A spinal nerve begins where the dorsal root (sensory axons) and the ventral root (motor axons) join, so from that point it carries both kinds of axon side by side.
options: Correct. The two roots join to form it.
Each axon carries action potentials in one direction only. The nerve is mixed because it holds two kinds of axons, not two-way axons.
Nerves do hold both myelinated and unmyelinated axons, but "mixed" refers to sensory plus motor axons.
Every spinal nerve does carry some autonomic axons, but that is not why it is called mixed.

why.correct: Pain along the sciatic path, numbness in the S1 dermatome (little toe, outer foot) and weak plantar flexion all fit the S1 root, usually pressed by a herniated disc. That picture is called sciatica.
options: The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps and the front of the thigh; his knee extension is normal and his pain is at the back.
The L4 root supplies the inner leg below the knee and helps knee extension, both normal here.
Correct. The S1 dermatome and weak plantar flexion point to the S1 root.
The common fibular nerve causes foot drop and numbness on the top of the foot, and it would not explain pain in the buttock and thigh.

why.correct: The trigeminal nerve (V) is the thick root on the side of the pons, the largest cranial nerve.
options: The facial nerve (VII) emerges lower, at the border between the pons and the medulla oblongata.
Correct. The thick root from the side of the pons is the trigeminal nerve.
The abducens nerve (VI) is a thin nerve near the midline at the lower border of the pons.
The vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) emerges beside the facial nerve at the pons–medulla border, below this root.

why.correct: The vagus nerve (X) leaves the side of the medulla oblongata as a row of rootlets, just below the glossopharyngeal nerve.
options: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) leaves the medulla just above the vagus rootlets.
The hypoglossal nerve (XII) leaves the front of the medulla, closer to the midline.
Correct. This is the vagus nerve, cranial nerve X.
The accessory nerve (XI) runs up alongside the medulla from the spinal cord, below and outside the vagus rootlets.

why.correct: The abducens nerve (VI) is the thin nerve leaving near the midline at the lower border of the pons. It supplies the eye muscle that turns the eye outward.
options: Correct. This is the abducens nerve, VI.
The trochlear nerve (IV) is a very thin nerve that curves around the side of the midbrain, higher up.
The oculomotor nerve (III) leaves the front of the midbrain, above the pons.
The facial nerve (VII) leaves the side of the brainstem at the pons–medulla border, farther from the midline.

why.correct: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) leaves the front of the medulla oblongata as a row of rootlets and supplies the muscles of the tongue.
options: The vagus nerve (X) leaves the side of the medulla, farther from the midline.
The accessory nerve (XI) rises from the spinal cord alongside the medulla, lower and more to the side.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) leaves the upper side of the medulla, above the vagus.
Correct. The rootlets at the front of the medulla form the hypoglossal nerve.

why.correct: The oculomotor nerve (III) leaves the front of the midbrain, between the cerebral peduncles, just behind the optic nerves.
options: The optic nerves (II) are the thick nerves that cross in an X in front of the midbrain.
Correct. This is the oculomotor nerve, III.
The trochlear nerve (IV) is thinner and wraps around the side of the midbrain from behind.
The olfactory nerves (I) lie under the frontal lobes, far forward.

why.correct: The facial nerve (VII) leaves the side of the brainstem at the border between the pons and the medulla oblongata, beside the vestibulocochlear nerve.
options: The trigeminal nerve (V) is the thicker root higher up, on the side of the pons.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) leaves the medulla, below this level.
Correct. This is the facial nerve, VII.
The abducens nerve (VI) leaves nearer the midline at the same level.

why.correct: The three purely sensory cranial nerves carry smell (I), vision (II), and hearing and balance (VIII).
options: Yes. The olfactory nerve carries only smell.
Yes. The optic nerve carries only vision.
No. The trigeminal nerve is both: it carries feeling from the face and supplies the chewing muscles.
Yes. The vestibulocochlear nerve carries only hearing and balance.
No. The hypoglossal nerve is motor, to the tongue muscles.
No. The oculomotor nerve is motor, to most eye muscles, with parasympathetic axons.

why.correct: Optic is II, trochlear IV, facial VII, glossopharyngeal IX and hypoglossal XII. The numbers follow the order in which the nerves attach, from front to back along the underside of the brain.
options: Optic nerve: II.
Trochlear nerve: IV.
Facial nerve: VII.
Glossopharyngeal nerve: IX.
Hypoglossal nerve: XII.

why.correct: The facial nerve (VII) supplies all the muscles of facial expression, including the forehead, the orbicularis oculi and the muscles around the mouth. Normal touch on the cheek shows the trigeminal nerve is working. This picture is typical of Bell’s palsy.
options: The trigeminal nerve carries feeling from the face and moves the chewing muscles. Her feeling is normal, and the trigeminal nerve does not move the brow, the muscle that closes the eye, or the mouth.
Correct. Paralysis of the whole half face with normal feeling points to the facial nerve.
The oculomotor nerve raises the upper lid and moves the eye, but it does not close the eye or move the forehead or mouth.
The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue, not the face.

why.correct: The oculomotor nerve (III) moves the eye up, down and in, raises the upper lid, and carries the parasympathetic axons that narrow the center of the eye in light. With III lost, the two eye muscles still working (supplied by IV and VI) pull the eye down and out.
options: Abducens damage leaves the eye turned in, not out, and does not affect the lid or the response to light.
Trochlear damage causes double vision looking down, but no drooping lid or wide center of the eye.
Correct. All three signs fit the oculomotor nerve.
Optic nerve damage causes loss of vision in that eye. It would not move the eye out of position or lower the lid.

why.correct: Each hypoglossal nerve supplies its own half of the tongue, and each half pushes its side forward. When the right nerve fails, the left half pushes harder and turns the tongue toward the weak right side.
options: A weak left side would let the right half push harder, turning the tongue to the left.
The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and touch from the back of the tongue; it does not move the tongue.
The glossopharyngeal nerve does not move the tongue on either side.
Correct. The tongue points toward the side of the damaged hypoglossal nerve.

why.correct: The abducens nerve (VI) supplies the muscle that turns the eye outward. Looking left needs the left eye to turn outward, which fails, so the two eyes point in different directions and he sees double.
options: Correct. The left eye cannot abduct, so the left abducens nerve is affected.
The right abducens nerve turns the right eye outward, which is needed for looking right, not left.
The oculomotor nerve turns the eye inward, up and down, not outward.
The trochlear nerve supplies the muscle that turns the eye down, most strongly when it points toward the nose, and its damage causes double vision looking down.

why.correct: The accessory nerve (XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid, which turns the head, and the trapezius, which shrugs the shoulder and helps swing the arm overhead. After it passes the sternocleidomastoid, it crosses the side of the neck just under the skin to reach the trapezius. Surgery there weakens the trapezius but usually spares head turning.
options: The phrenic nerve runs to the diaphragm; it does not move the shoulder.
The vagus nerve supplies the throat, voice box and organs of the chest and abdomen, not the trapezius.
Correct. A drooping shoulder and a weak shrug point to the accessory nerve’s supply to the trapezius.
The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue, not the neck and shoulder.

why.correct: About three quarters of all parasympathetic axons travel in the vagus nerves, which supply the heart, lungs and most digestive organs.
options: The facial nerve carries parasympathetic axons only to the tear glands and two pairs of saliva glands.
The glossopharyngeal nerve carries parasympathetic axons only to the largest saliva gland.
The oculomotor nerve carries parasympathetic axons only to muscles inside the eye.
Correct. The vagus nerve carries most parasympathetic output, including to the heart.

why.correct: The vagus nerve is both motor and sensory. It supplies the throat and voice box, sends parasympathetic output to the heart, lungs and digestive organs, and carries sensory signals back from those organs.
options: Yes. Vagal acetylcholine slows the heart’s pacemaker.
Yes. The vagus nerve supplies all the muscles of the voice box, so damage makes the voice hoarse.
Yes. Most vagal axons are sensory, carrying signals such as stomach stretch to the brainstem.
No. The tongue is moved by the hypoglossal nerve.
Yes. Vagal parasympathetic output increases gut muscle activity and gland secretion.
No. Closing the eyes is done by the orbicularis oculi, supplied by the facial nerve.

why.correct: The maxillary division (V2) carries feeling from the cheek, upper lip, upper teeth and palate.
options: The forehead belongs to the ophthalmic division (V1).
Correct. That is the area of the maxillary division.
The lower lip, chin and lower teeth belong to the mandibular division (V3).
Taste from the front of the tongue is carried by the facial nerve, not the trigeminal.

why.correct: The touch travels in on the trigeminal nerve (V1) of the side touched, and the blink goes out on both facial nerves. Touching the right eye makes both eyes blink, so both facial nerves work. Only the left touch fails, so the left trigeminal input is lost.
options: If the left facial nerve were damaged, touching the right eye would make only the right eye blink. Here both eyes blink.
If the right facial nerve were damaged, the right eye would fail to blink whichever eye was touched.
Correct. The left trigeminal nerve cannot carry the touch in, so no blink is triggered.
The oculomotor nerve raises the upper lid; it does not close the eye or carry touch.

why.correct: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) carries touch from the upper throat and the back of the tongue to the medulla. The vagus nerve (X) then drives the throat muscles.
options: The hypoglossal nerve is motor to the tongue; it carries no touch in.
The trigeminal nerve carries touch from the face and the front of the mouth, not the back of the throat.
The accessory nerve is motor to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
Correct. IX carries the touch in and X carries the command out.

why.correct: The trigeminal nerve carries feeling from the face and supplies the chewing muscles. Facial expression belongs to the facial nerve.
options: Correct pairing. The olfactory nerve carries smell.
Correct pairing. The optic nerve carries vision.
This is the wrong pairing. Facial expression is the facial nerve; the trigeminal nerve feels the face and moves the jaw.
Correct pairing. The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance.
Correct pairing. The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue.

why.correct: IX, X and XI all pass through the jugular foramen at the base of the skull.
options: The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves enter the internal acoustic meatus; only IX uses the jugular foramen.
These three eye muscle nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure.
Correct. Glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory share the jugular foramen.
The hypoglossal nerve has its own opening, the hypoglossal canal.

why.correct: The short olfactory axons pass up through the holes of the cribriform plate. A blow to the head, most often to the back, can shear them there. Much of flavor is smell, so food tastes flat.
options: The optic nerve carries vision; its damage would affect sight, not smell.
Correct. Shearing of the olfactory axons at the cribriform plate causes loss of smell.
Facial nerve damage could reduce taste from the front of the tongue, but it would not stop him smelling coffee.
The trigeminal nerve carries touch from the face; it does not carry smell.

why.correct: The trochlear nerve (IV) supplies the one eye muscle that turns the eye down, most strongly when the eye points toward the nose: the position used for reading and looking at stairs.
options: Abducens damage causes double vision looking to the side, not down.
Oculomotor damage would usually also cause a drooping lid and a wide center of the eye, which she does not have.
Optic nerve damage reduces vision itself rather than causing double vision.
Correct. Double vision looking down, eased by tilting the head, fits the trochlear nerve.

why.correct: Parasympathetic axons travel in III, VII, IX and X ("1973").
options: Yes. III narrows the center of the eye and adjusts focus for near vision.
No. The trigeminal nerve has no parasympathetic axons of its own, though some ride along its branches after leaving other nerves.
Yes. VII supplies the tear glands and two pairs of saliva glands.
Yes. IX supplies the largest saliva gland.
Yes. X supplies the heart, lungs and most digestive organs.
No. The accessory nerve is motor to two neck and shoulder muscles.

why.correct: The facial nerve (VII) carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue.
options: The trigeminal nerve carries touch, not taste, from the front of the tongue.
Correct. Taste from the front two-thirds travels in the facial nerve.
The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the back third of the tongue.
The hypoglossal nerve is motor to the tongue muscles and carries no taste.

why.correct: The vagus nerve supplies the muscles that lift the back of the roof of the mouth and the muscles of the voice box. The right side stays low because the right vagus nerve is damaged, and the healthy left side pulls the tag toward itself. Voice box weakness makes the voice hoarse.
options: If the left vagus were damaged, the left side would stay low and the tag would be pulled to the right.
Correct. The right side fails to rise and the voice is hoarse: right vagus nerve.
The glossopharyngeal nerve mainly carries sensation from the throat; it does not lift the roof of the mouth or move the voice box.
The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue; its damage makes the tongue point to one side, not the roof of the mouth.

why.correct: The medial lemniscus is the ribbon of crossed second-order axons of the dorsal column pathway, climbing from the medulla oblongata to the thalamus.
options: The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature; in this figure it is the separate bundle drawn on the other pathway.
The fasciculus cuneatus is a bundle of first-order axons in the dorsal column of the spinal cord, below the medulla.
Correct. After crossing in the medulla, the second-order axons form the medial lemniscus.
The internal capsule is the band of white matter between the thalamus and the cortex, above the brainstem.

why.correct: The first-order neuron runs from the fingertip up the same side of the cord to the medulla. The second-order neuron crosses there and rises in the medial lemniscus to the thalamus. The third-order neuron reaches the somatosensory cortex of the opposite hemisphere.
options: Transduction happens first, at the sensory receptor.
The first-order neuron’s cell body is in the dorsal root ganglion; its axon enters through the dorsal root.
Axons from the arm run in the fasciculus cuneatus, on the same side, with no synapse in the cord.
The first synapse is in the nucleus cuneatus of the lower medulla.
The second-order axon crosses in the medulla and forms the medial lemniscus.
The thalamus relays the signal to the primary somatosensory cortex.

why.correct: The lateral spinothalamic tract is the bundle of crossed second-order axons carrying pain and temperature up the side of the cord opposite the body part.
options: The fasciculus gracilis lies in the dorsal column, at the back of the cord, and carries fine touch from the lower body.
Correct. This is the lateral spinothalamic tract.
The medial lemniscus is in the brainstem, not the spinal cord.
The dorsal root is outside the cord, entering at the back.

why.correct: The fasciculus gracilis is the part of the dorsal column nearest the midline. It carries fine touch, vibration and position from the lower body, below about T6.
options: Correct. The medial bundle of the dorsal column is the fasciculus gracilis.
The fasciculus cuneatus lies lateral to it and carries signals from the upper body and arm.
The spinothalamic tract runs in the lateral and anterior columns, not at the back of the cord.
The spinocerebellar tracts run in the lateral columns toward the cerebellum.

why.correct: The dorsal column pathway climbs on the same side and crosses only in the medulla, so the cut removes vibration and position from the left. Pain and temperature axons cross within a segment or two of entering, so the left spinothalamic tract carries signals from the right, and those are lost on the right.
options: This would need both pathways to run on the left, but the spinothalamic axons in the left cord serve the right side of the body.
This would need both pathways to have crossed below T10, but dorsal column axons do not cross until the medulla.
This reverses the two pathways. Pain and temperature cross early, so the left tract serves the right side.
Correct. Dorsal column loss is on the same side; spinothalamic loss is on the opposite side.

why.correct: The channel opened by capsaicin and by damaging heat is found on nociceptors, free nerve endings that detect harmful stimuli. That is why chili "burns" without any heat.
options: Correct. Capsaicin stimulates nociceptors, which respond to heat intense enough to damage tissue.
Mechanoreceptors respond to physical deformation such as touch and stretch, not to chemicals or heat.
A photoreceptor responds to light and sits in the eye.
Osmoreceptors respond to the solute concentration of body fluids, in the hypothalamus.

why.correct: Stimulus strength is coded by the frequency of action potentials and by the number of neurons firing, not by the size of each action potential.

variables.name: Size of the graded receptor potential in the ending
variables.why: A stronger deformation opens more mechanically gated channels, so more Na+ enters and the graded depolarization is larger.

variables.name: Height of each action potential
variables.why: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached, each one peaks at the same voltage.

variables.name: Number of action potentials per second
variables.why: The larger receptor potential holds the trigger zone further above threshold, so each new action potential fires sooner after the last.

variables.name: Number of nearby sensory neurons firing
variables.why: A harder press deforms a wider patch of skin and reaches higher-threshold endings, recruiting more neurons.

why.correct: The anesthetic leaves transduction intact but stops conduction along the axon, so nociception at the ending never becomes a perception.

variables.name: Receptor potentials in the nociceptor endings in the tooth
variables.why: The drilling still opens channels in the endings, which lie beyond the blocked stretch of nerve, so receptor potentials still form.

variables.name: Action potentials reaching the brainstem from the tooth
variables.why: Action potentials need voltage-gated sodium channels to regenerate along the axon. Where the channels are blocked, conduction fails.

variables.name: Pain perceived from the tooth
variables.why: Without signals reaching the brainstem, thalamus and cortex, no pain is perceived, even though the tissue is being stimulated.

why.correct: Phasic, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors such as tactile corpuscles and hair follicle endings fire when a stimulus starts and fall silent while it holds steady, so the steady pressure of socks stops being reported.
options: The socks still press on the skin; what changes is the response of the sensory receptors, not the stimulus.
Correct. Phasic mechanoreceptors adapt to a steady stimulus.
Socks do not stimulate nociceptors, which respond to harmful stimuli, and nociceptors adapt very little anyway.
The dorsal columns keep conducting whatever signals arrive; the drop happens at the sensory receptors and at synapses along the way.

why.correct: Nociceptors are tonic, slowly adapting sensory receptors: they keep firing for as long as the damaging stimulus, here the chemicals from injured tissue, is present.
options: Correct. Nociceptors adapt very little.
Pain travels in the spinothalamic tract, not the dorsal columns.
Nociceptors are free nerve endings, with no capsule.
The ring fades because the touch endings adapt, not because the thalamus selects between the two.

why.correct: Visceral pain axons from the heart enter the cord at about T1 to T4, the same segments that receive skin axons from the chest and inner arm. They converge on shared second-order neurons, and the brain assigns the pain to the skin that line usually reports.
options: No nerves run from the heart into the arm; the arm pain is referred, not local.
A heart attack does not stretch the arm’s vessels, and his arm is healthy.
Correct. This is referred pain, explained by convergence in the dorsal horn.
The phrenic nerve carries sensation from the diaphragm and causes shoulder-tip pain, not inner arm pain from the heart.

why.correct: The diaphragm’s sensory axons run in the phrenic nerve to C3 to C5, which also supply the skin over the shoulder. Irritation of the diaphragm is therefore referred to the shoulder tip.
options: T1 to T4 receive heart pain, referred to the chest and inner arm.
Correct. The phrenic nerve enters the cord at C3 to C5, which also supply the shoulder skin.
T10 to L1 receive signals from organs such as the appendix and kidney, referred to the navel, flank and groin.
L4 to S1 supply the leg and foot.

why.correct: Second-order pain and temperature axons cross the midline in front of the central canal, within a segment or two of entry. A central cavity cuts these crossing axons from both sides at the levels it spans, while the dorsal columns, off to the back, are spared.
options: If the dorsal columns were destroyed, fine touch and vibration would be lost, but they are normal.
The dorsal root ganglia lie outside the cord in the intervertebral foramina; a cavity inside the cord cannot reach them.
Nociceptors in the skin are not affected by damage inside the spinal cord.
Correct. A central cord cavity cuts the crossing spinothalamic axons.

why.correct: Pain and temperature axons from the left face descend on the left in the medulla before their second-order neurons cross. The spinothalamic axons from the right body crossed back in the spinal cord and now run on the left. One lesion on the left side of the medulla catches both.
options: Correct. Uncrossed face fibers and already-crossed body fibers run side by side in the lateral medulla.
Spinothalamic axons cross in the spinal cord, not the medulla, so the body loss is on the side opposite the damage while the face loss is on the same side.
The facial nerve moves the face; feeling from the face travels in the trigeminal nerve. No nerve outside the brain was damaged.
The dorsal columns carry fine touch and vibration, not pain and temperature.

why.correct: The dorsal column pathway carries fine touch, two-point discrimination, vibration and conscious proprioception. Pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic tract.
options: Yes. Vibration from lamellated corpuscles travels in the dorsal columns.
Yes. Precise touch and two-point discrimination use the dorsal columns.
No. Pain travels in the spinothalamic tract.
Yes. Conscious proprioception travels in the dorsal columns.
No. Temperature travels in the spinothalamic tract.

why.correct: The first-order neuron synapses in the dorsal horn, and the second-order axon crosses in front of the central canal within a segment or two, then climbs on the opposite side.
options: The dorsal column pathway crosses in the medulla; the spinothalamic tract has already crossed by then.
The thalamus is where the second-order neuron ends, not where it crosses.
Correct. Spinothalamic axons cross in the spinal cord close to their level of entry.
The internal capsule carries third-order axons from the thalamus to the cortex; no crossing happens there.

why.correct: After the synapse in the dorsal horn, the second-order axon crosses within a segment or two and rises in the opposite spinothalamic tract to the thalamus.
options: The dorsal column carries fine touch and position, and its first-order axons do not synapse in the dorsal horn.
Correct. The crossed second-order axon climbs in the left spinothalamic tract.
The medial lemniscus carries the dorsal column pathway, and it rises on the side opposite the body part, not the same side.
The third-order neuron runs from the thalamus to the cortex; it does not cross in the medulla.

why.correct: In the dorsal column pathway, the first-order axon does not synapse in the dorsal horn. It climbs the dorsal column all the way to the medulla. Synapsing in the dorsal horn is what the spinothalamic tract does.
options: Correct step. Tactile corpuscles detect light touch.
Correct step. Signals from the sole enter through sacral dorsal roots.
This is the wrong step. Dorsal column first-order axons rise without synapsing until the medulla.
Correct step. Axons from the lower body run in the fasciculus gracilis on the same side.
Correct step. The second-order axon crosses in the medulla and forms the medial lemniscus.
Correct step. The thalamus relays to the somatosensory cortex of the opposite hemisphere.

why.correct: They sit in an internal organ, so they are interoceptors, and they respond to stretch, a physical deformation, so they are mechanoreceptors.
options: Exteroceptors respond to stimuli from outside the body, and stretch is not a chemical stimulus.
Proprioceptors are in muscles, tendons and joints, and stretch is not temperature.
They are interoceptors, but ordinary filling is not a damaging stimulus, so they are not nociceptors.
Correct. Internal location, stretch stimulus: interoceptor and mechanoreceptor.

why.correct: Sensation is the detection of a stimulus and its delivery into the CNS. These signals are delivered to the brainstem and used there, but they are not relayed to the cortex for conscious interpretation, so there is no perception.
options: The stretch-sensitive endings in artery walls are slowly adapting; they keep reporting pressure.
Correct. The brainstem uses the signals without any conscious perception.
These signals travel in cranial nerves to the brainstem, not in the spinal cord’s dorsal columns, and the dorsal columns do reach awareness.
These signals do not pass through the spinal cord at all; they travel in cranial nerves straight to the brainstem.

why.correct: Vibration and joint position travel in the dorsal columns, and both legs are affected. With position sense gone, she relies on vision to stay balanced, so she sways with her eyes closed. Pain and temperature, in the spinothalamic tracts, are spared.
options: Correct. Both dorsal columns carry vibration and position from the legs.
Damage to the spinothalamic tracts would remove pain and temperature, which are normal.
A left thalamic lesion would remove sensation from the whole right side, not both legs, and would include pain.
The cerebellum coordinates movement but does not produce conscious loss of vibration sense.

why.correct: By the time sensory pathways reach the thalamus, every one of them, from the body and from the face, has crossed. The right thalamus therefore relays all sensation from the left side of the body and face.
options: The right thalamus serves the left side, because all pathways have crossed below it.
The face pathway and the body pathways both pass through the thalamus, so the body would be affected too.
A split pattern like this arises in the spinal cord, where the two pathways cross at different levels, not in the thalamus.
Correct. Above the medulla all pathways have crossed, so the loss is on the whole opposite side.

why.correct: The modality you perceive depends on which pathway is active, not on the stimulus. Pressure fires neurons of the vision pathway, and signals on that line are perceived as light. This is the labeled line principle.
options: No light is produced; the signal is triggered by pressure.
Correct. Any signal on the vision pathway is perceived as light.
If touch endings were responsible, you would feel pressure, not see light.
Adaptation would make a sensation fade; it does not explain seeing light.

why.correct: Myelinated nociceptive axons conduct quickly and carry sharp, well-localized fast pain. Unmyelinated axons conduct slowly and carry burning or aching slow pain, which arrives later and lasts longer.
options: Both kinds of pain travel in the spinothalamic tract.
The toe is not an internal organ, and both waves come from the injured toe.
Correct. Two kinds of axon with different conduction speeds.
The refractory period lasts milliseconds and would not produce a second wave a second later with a different quality.

why.correct: The spinocerebellar tracts carry signals from muscles and joints to the cerebellum on the same side. The cerebellum uses them to coordinate movement, and they are never consciously perceived.
options: Correct. Unconscious proprioception goes to the ipsilateral cerebellum.
That route, through the thalamus to the cortex, is the dorsal column pathway, which carries conscious proprioception.
The hypothalamus receives temperature information, not proprioception from muscles.
The spinocerebellar tracts do not end in the medulla or reach the cortex.

why.correct: The first-order neurons for the face have their cell bodies in the trigeminal ganglion, the cranial nerve equivalent of a dorsal root ganglion.
options: Cervical dorsal root ganglia serve the neck and arm, not the face.
Correct. The trigeminal ganglion holds the first-order cell bodies for the face.
The thalamus holds the third-order cell bodies.
The postcentral gyrus is where the third-order axons end.

why.correct: Every command to a skeletal muscle, from the cortex, the brainstem or a spinal circuit, must pass through the lower motor neuron, because only its axon leaves the CNS and reaches the muscle fibers.
options: An upper motor neuron's axon stays inside the CNS and ends on lower motor neurons or interneurons. It never reaches the muscle.
Correct. The lower motor neuron is the only route out to the muscle, so it is the final common path.
Dorsal horn interneurons handle incoming sensory signals. They do not send axons to muscle.
The red nucleus holds upper motor neurons of the rubrospinal tract, which end on lower motor neurons in the cord.

why.correct: The upper motor neuron's axon leaves the left precentral gyrus, funnels through the internal capsule, runs in the cerebral peduncle, forms part of the pyramid on the front of the medulla, crosses at the pyramidal decussation, descends in the right lateral corticospinal tract and synapses on a lower motor neuron in the right ventral horn of the cervical enlargement.

About 85–90% cross in the lower medulla and form the lateral corticospinal tract. The remaining 10–15% descend uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract, and most of those cross later in the cord.
options: That is the share that does not cross at the decussation: the anterior corticospinal tract.
The split is far from even. The large majority cross in the medulla.
Correct. Most corticospinal axons cross at the pyramidal decussation.
Not every axon crosses here. The anterior corticospinal tract, about 10–15% of the axons, stays uncrossed in the medulla.

why.correct: The internal capsule lies above the pyramidal decussation. The corticospinal axons there have not crossed yet, and they are on their way to cross in the lower medulla and control the right side. Losing them weakens the right side.
options: Same-side weakness follows damage below the pyramidal decussation, in the spinal cord. The internal capsule is above it.
Correct. Damage above the decussation weakens the opposite side.
Each internal capsule carries axons for the opposite side only. Weakness on both sides would need damage on both sides.
The axons of the upper motor neurons pass through the internal capsule. Cutting them stops the signal, even though their cell bodies in the cortex survive.

why.correct: The lateral corticospinal tract runs in the lateral white column and carries the crossed corticospinal axons to lower motor neurons for the limbs.
options: Correct. This is the lateral corticospinal tract, in the lateral white column.
The anterior corticospinal tract lies in the anterior column, beside the anterior median fissure.
The spinothalamic tract is ascending: it carries pain and temperature up the cord in the lateral and anterior columns.
The dorsal column fills the posterior column and carries fine touch and position up to the medulla.

why.correct: Flaccidity, lost tendon jerks, marked atrophy and fasciculations are lower motor neuron signs. The lower motor neuron's cell body is in the ventral horn, and its axon leaves through the ventral root.
options: Motor cortex damage is upper motor neuron damage. After the first days it produces stiffness and brisk tendon jerks, not wasting with twitches.
The internal capsule carries upper motor neuron axons. Damage there causes spastic weakness of the opposite side.
The lateral corticospinal tract is made of upper motor neuron axons. Cutting it leaves the lower motor neurons healthy, so there are no fasciculations and little wasting.
Correct. These are the signs of a lower motor neuron lesion.

why.correct: Upper motor neuron damage frees the lower motor neurons and spinal circuits from descending control: tone rises (spasticity), tendon jerks become brisk and the big toe goes up when the sole is stroked.
options: Correct. Spasticity is raised tone that grows with the speed of stretch.
Fasciculations come from sick lower motor neurons firing by themselves. With upper motor neuron damage the lower motor neurons are healthy.
Correct. Released spinal circuits make tendon jerks abnormally brisk.
Correct. An upward big toe in an adult signals corticospinal damage.
Marked, fast wasting follows loss of the muscle's nerve supply, which is lower motor neuron damage. Upper motor neuron damage causes only slow disuse thinning.
Upper motor neuron damage can cause a floppy limb for the first days or weeks, but it then turns spastic. Lasting flaccidity points to the lower motor neuron.

why.correct: The forehead part of the facial nucleus gets corticobulbar input from both hemispheres, while the lower face part gets it mainly from the opposite hemisphere. Upper motor neuron damage on the left therefore spares the right forehead and weakens only the lower right face. The facial nerve is the lower motor neuron for the whole half of the face, so damage to it weakens everything on that side.
options: This is the reverse. Facial nerve damage weakens the forehead too, and cortex damage spares it.
Sparing of the forehead is not a matter of severity. Any facial nerve damage that weakens the lower face also reaches the forehead, because one nerve supplies both.
Correct. A has an upper motor neuron lesion on the left; B has a lower motor neuron lesion on the right.
The corticobulbar input to the lower face comes from the opposite hemisphere, so right-sided face weakness points to the left cortex, and it points to the right facial nerve, not the left.

why.correct: Damage to one half of the cord removes the motor tract and dorsal column for the same side, both of which crossed higher up, and the spinothalamic tract carrying pain from the opposite side, which crossed at entry. The result: same-side upper motor neuron weakness and loss of position sense, opposite-side loss of pain and temperature.

variables.name: Voluntary strength of the right leg
variables.why: The right lateral corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla and carries commands for the right leg, so cutting it at T8 weakens the right leg.

variables.name: Muscle tone and tendon jerks in the right leg
variables.why: The right leg's lower motor neurons below T8 survive but lose descending control, so after the early floppy phase tone and tendon jerks increase.

variables.name: Vibration and position sense in the right leg
variables.why: The right dorsal column carries fine touch, vibration and position from the right side and does not cross until the medulla.

variables.name: Pain and temperature sense in the right leg
variables.why: Pain from the right leg crosses in the cord near where it enters and climbs in the left spinothalamic tract, which is intact.

variables.name: Pain and temperature sense in the left leg
variables.why: Pain from the left leg crosses within a segment or two and climbs in the right spinothalamic tract, which is cut.

variables.name: Voluntary strength of the left leg
variables.why: Commands for the left leg descend in the left lateral corticospinal tract, which is intact.

why.correct: Loss of upper motor neurons in the left cortex weakens the right arm and lower right face, with spasticity and brisk tendon jerks appearing over the following weeks. The forehead is spared because of its input from both hemispheres, and muscle bulk is kept because the lower motor neurons survive.

variables.name: Strength of the right arm
variables.why: The upper motor neurons for the right arm are in the left precentral gyrus, and their axons cross at the pyramidal decussation.

variables.name: Tendon jerks in the right arm
variables.why: The right arm's lower motor neurons are healthy but lose descending control, so after the early floppy phase their tendon jerks become brisk.

variables.name: Strength of the lower right face
variables.why: The lower face part of the right facial nucleus receives corticobulbar input mainly from the left hemisphere.

variables.name: Strength of the right forehead
variables.why: The forehead part of the facial nucleus also receives input from the right hemisphere, which is undamaged.

variables.name: Strength of the left arm
variables.why: The left arm is driven by the right motor cortex, which is undamaged.

variables.name: Muscle bulk of the right arm
variables.why: Lower motor neurons still supply the muscle, so there is no fast wasting; at most slight disuse thinning over months.

why.correct: In infants the corticospinal axons are not yet fully myelinated, so the upward big toe is normal. It changes to the adult downward response by about 1 to 2 years of age.
options: In an adult this would be the Babinski sign of corticospinal damage, but in a 9-month-old it is expected.
Lower motor neuron damage would weaken the toe muscles or remove the response altogether, not produce an upward toe.
Correct. The upward big toe is normal until the corticospinal tract matures.
An upward toe is an active extension, not a failure of the flexors. It reflects the maturity of the descending control, not muscle strength.

why.correct: The vestibulospinal tract runs uncrossed from the vestibular nuclei, which receive balance signals from the balance organs deep in the skull, to motor neurons for the extensor muscles of the trunk and legs.
options: The tectospinal tract, from the superior colliculus, turns the head and neck toward a sudden sight or sound.
Correct. Balance signals drive posture through the vestibulospinal tract.
The rubrospinal tract, from the red nucleus, helps drive flexor muscles of the arm and is small in humans.
The anterior corticospinal tract carries voluntary commands from the cortex to neck and trunk muscles. It does not carry the balance signals that correct a tip.

why.correct: Dopamine favors movement by boosting the direct pathway and damping the indirect one. Without it, the brake from the globus pallidus on the thalamus presses harder, and movement becomes slow and hard to begin.

variables.name: Activity of the direct (go) pathway
variables.why: Dopamine normally excites the direct-pathway striatal neurons, so losing it weakens them.

variables.name: Activity of the indirect (stop) pathway
variables.why: Dopamine normally inhibits the indirect-pathway striatal neurons, so losing it frees them.

variables.name: Inhibition of the thalamus by the globus pallidus output
variables.why: Less direct-pathway inhibition and more indirect-pathway excitation both make the globus pallidus output fire more.

variables.name: Ease of starting a movement
variables.why: A more inhibited thalamus excites the motor cortex less, so movements are slow, small and hard to start.

why.correct: Intention tremor, overshooting (dysmetria) and clumsy rapid alternating movements with normal strength are cerebellar signs. Cerebellar damage shows on the same side, and the lateral hemisphere handles skilled limb movement, so the right cerebellar hemisphere is the likely site.
options: The cerebellum's output crosses and the corticospinal tract crosses back, so each side of the cerebellum coordinates the same side of the body. Left cerebellar damage would affect the left hand.
Correct. Same-side cerebellar signs with normal strength point here.
Substantia nigra damage causes a tremor at rest and slowness, not a tremor that grows near a target.
Cutting the corticospinal tract causes weakness. His grip is strong.

why.correct: The vermis is the narrow midline strip joining the two cerebellar hemispheres. With the strip beside it, it forms the spinocerebellum, which controls posture and corrects movement as it happens.
options: Correct. This is the vermis.
The hemispheres are the large lateral parts on either side of the vermis.
The flocculonodular lobe is the small lobe on the underside: a nodule in the midline and a flocculus on each side.
The peduncles are white matter stalks connecting the cerebellum to the brainstem, not a region of the cerebellar surface.

why.correct: The globus pallidus output is itself inhibitory and fires all the time. When the striatum inhibits it, it fires less, so the thalamus is inhibited less, not more. Removing that brake frees the thalamus to excite the cortex.
options: This step is right. Cortical input to the striatum is excitatory.
This step is right. Direct-pathway striatal neurons are inhibitory and act on the globus pallidus output.
This is the error. An inhibited globus pallidus inhibits the thalamus less: the brake is released.
This step is right. A released thalamus excites the motor cortex.

why.correct: The middle cerebellar peduncle, the largest, joins the pons and carries the relayed copy of the cortex's motor plan into the cerebellum.
options: The internal capsule is a band of axons deep in each cerebral hemisphere, not a connection of the cerebellum.
The corpus callosum joins the two cerebral hemispheres to each other.
The cerebral peduncles are stalks on the front of the midbrain that carry the corticospinal axons down. They do not enter the cerebellum.
Correct. The middle peduncle carries input from the pons.

why.correct: Wasting and fasciculations are lower motor neuron signs; brisk tendon jerks and Babinski signs are upper motor neuron signs. Normal sensation means the sensory pathways are spared. A disease that destroys both kinds of motor neuron, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, produces exactly this mixture.
options: Dorsal column damage would remove vibration and position sense, and sensation here is normal.
Correct. Both motor neuron types are affected, and sensation is spared.
Cerebellar damage causes clumsiness with normal strength and no wasting, twitching or Babinski sign.
Damage to the arm nerves would explain the hands, but not the brisk knee jerks and upward toes, and it would usually affect sensation too.

why.correct: At the junction of the medulla and spinal cord, most corticospinal axons cross the midline in the pyramidal decussation (the decussation of the pyramids) and continue as the lateral corticospinal tract.
options: Correct. This is where most corticospinal axons cross.
The cerebral peduncle is higher up, on the front of the midbrain.
The anterior corticospinal tract is the uncrossed bundle running down beside the anterior median fissure of the cord.
The internal capsule lies deep in the cerebral hemisphere, well above the medulla.

why.correct: The sensory receptor detects the stimulus, the sensory neuron carries the signal into the CNS, the integration center passes it on through one or more synapses, the motor neuron carries it out, and the effector responds.
options: The sensory receptor comes first: it turns the stimulus into a graded receptor potential.
The sensory neuron carries action potentials from the sensory receptor into the CNS.
The integration center, in the gray matter of the cord or brainstem, links the sensory neuron to the motor neuron.
The motor neuron carries the output from the CNS to the effector.
The effector, a muscle or gland, produces the response last.

why.correct: Between the sensory and motor neurons lies the integration center: one or more synapses in the gray matter of the spinal cord or brainstem.
options: The dorsal root ganglion holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons. It is part of the sensory neuron, not the link to the motor neuron.
Correct. The integration center passes the signal from sensory to motor neurons.
The neuromuscular junction is where the motor neuron meets the effector, after the motor neuron in the sequence.
The primary motor cortex starts voluntary movements. A spinal reflex does not need to pass through it.

why.correct: Normal voluntary strength means the motor neurons, ventral roots and muscle all work. Lost feeling plus a lost reflex points to the sensory side of the arc: the dorsal root that carries both skin sensation and spindle signals from that region.
options: If the ventral root were cut, the quadriceps would be weak on voluntary effort too, and sensation would be normal.
A diseased quadriceps would be weak when he kicks on purpose, and it would not remove feeling from the skin.
Correct. The sensory side has failed while the motor side still works.
Damage to the ventral horn motor neurons would weaken voluntary kicking as well and would leave sensation intact.

why.correct: The stretch reflex is monosynaptic: the spindle sensory axons synapse directly on the quadriceps motor neurons. Interneurons are used only for the polysynaptic branch that inhibits the hamstrings.
options: Right step. The tap pushes in the ligament, which pulls on and stretches the quadriceps.
Right step. Muscle spindles are the stretch sensors.
Right step. Sensory axons enter through the dorsal roots of about L2 to L4.
This is the error. There is no interneuron between the spindle sensory axon and the motor neurons of the same muscle.
Right step. The motor neurons release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junctions.
Right step. Quadriceps contraction straightens the knee.

why.correct: The tap stretches the calf muscles through their tendon, and the muscle spindles in those muscles detect the stretch. Despite its name, every deep tendon reflex is a stretch reflex.
options: Golgi tendon organs sense tension from contraction, not a brief stretch, and they start a reflex that relaxes the muscle rather than contracting it.
Nociceptors respond to harmful stimuli. A reflex hammer tap is not painful, and nociceptors start the withdrawal reflex, which bends a limb.
Correct. Spindles sense the stretch and excite the calf motor neurons directly.
Touch sensors in the skin report contact, but they are not the sensory receptor for this reflex. It still works when the skin is numb.

why.correct: Only the stretch reflex's path to the stretched muscle itself is monosynaptic. Inhibiting an antagonist, withdrawal, crossing the midline and the tendon reflex all need interneurons.
options: No. The spindle sensory axons synapse directly on the quadriceps motor neurons: one synapse.
Yes. A sensory neuron can only excite, so inhibiting the hamstring motor neurons needs an inhibitory interneuron (reciprocal inhibition).
Yes. Nociceptor signals pass through interneurons that spread across several segments.
Yes. Interneurons carry the signal across the midline to the opposite limb.
Yes. The tendon organ's sensory neuron acts on the motor neurons through inhibitory interneurons.

why.correct: One painful stimulus drives opposite patterns in the two legs. The right leg bends and lifts (withdrawal reflex), and the left leg straightens to support the body (crossed-extensor reflex), all through interneurons in the cord.

variables.name: Motor neurons to the right leg's flexors
variables.why: Nociceptor signals excite interneurons that excite the flexor motor neurons of the stimulated limb: the withdrawal reflex.

variables.name: Motor neurons to the right leg's extensors
variables.why: Inhibitory interneurons silence the extensors of the same limb, so they do not resist the withdrawal.

variables.name: Motor neurons to the left leg's extensors
variables.why: Interneurons that cross the midline excite the extensors of the opposite limb: the crossed-extensor reflex.

variables.name: Motor neurons to the left leg's flexors
variables.why: Crossed inhibitory connections silence the opposite limb's flexors, so the left leg straightens and bears weight.

why.correct: The withdrawal reflex is integrated in the spinal cord, so the flexors contract without waiting for the brain. The same nociceptor signals climb the spinothalamic tract, and pain is felt only when they reach the cortex.
options: No decision is needed. A voluntary movement would take longer than the reflex, and the pain would have to arrive first.
Correct. The reflex and the perception run in parallel, and the reflex finishes first.
Heat does not make skeletal muscle contract. The movement needs nociceptors, sensory neurons, interneurons and motor neurons.
The cerebellum coordinates movement but does not detect heat or start reflexes. The withdrawal reflex runs in the cord.

why.correct: A visceral reflex acts on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or glands. Saliva comes from glands, driven by autonomic neurons.
options: The knee jerk acts on skeletal muscle (the quadriceps), so it is a somatic reflex.
The withdrawal reflex acts on skeletal muscles of the leg, so it is somatic.
Correct. Its effectors are glands, so it is visceral.
The crossed-extensor reflex acts on skeletal muscles, so it is somatic.

why.correct: A visceral reflex sends its output through a chain of two motor neurons, which synapse in a ganglion outside the CNS, to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or glands. A somatic reflex uses one motor neuron straight to skeletal muscle.
options: Correct. Two neurons and a ganglion on the way.
That describes the somatic reflex.
Both kinds have a sensory receptor and sensory neuron. They differ on the motor side.
The second axon of a visceral chain is unmyelinated, so visceral reflexes are slower than somatic ones.

why.correct: 4+ means very brisk with clonus. It points to upper motor neuron damage.
options: 1+ is a weak, diminished reflex.
2+ is normal.
3+ is brisker than average without clonus, and it may or may not be abnormal.
Correct. Clonus makes it 4+.

why.correct: Hyperreflexia with clonus, a Babinski sign and a stiff, weak leg are upper motor neuron signs. The reflex arcs are intact but have lost the descending control that normally damps them.
options: A broken sensory side of the arc would weaken or abolish the reflexes, not exaggerate them.
A damaged peripheral nerve breaks the arc and makes the reflexes weaker, with a floppy leg.
Losing ventral horn motor neurons removes the output of the arc, so reflexes fall and the muscle wastes.
Correct. The arcs are released from descending control.

why.correct: Cutting dorsal roots removes the sensory side of every arc that enters through them. Reflexes and skin sensation of those segments are lost, but voluntary strength remains because the motor side and the descending tracts are intact.

variables.name: Left knee jerk
variables.why: The spindle sensory axons from the quadriceps enter through these dorsal roots, so the arc's sensory side is broken.

variables.name: Voluntary strength of the left quadriceps
variables.why: Motor axons leave through the ventral roots, which are intact, and the corticospinal pathway is untouched.

variables.name: Skin sensation on the front of the left thigh and knee
variables.why: Those dermatomes send their sensory axons through the L2 to L4 dorsal roots.

variables.name: Left ankle jerk
variables.why: The ankle jerk runs through S1, whose roots are intact.

why.correct: Right after the cut, reflexes below it are absent. Over the next weeks they return and become exaggerated, because the reflex arcs are intact but freed from the brain's control. Voluntary movement and sensation stay lost, because both depend on tracts that pass through T6.

variables.name: Knee jerks
variables.why: On the day of the injury the reflexes below the cut are absent, but the arcs in the lumbar cord survive. Released from descending control, they return over days to weeks and become brisker than before.

variables.name: Voluntary movement of the legs
variables.why: Every descending motor tract is cut at T6, so no command from the brain reaches the lumbar motor neurons.

variables.name: Withdrawal of a foot from a pinprick
variables.why: The withdrawal reflex runs in the lumbar and sacral cord. After the early absent phase it returns, often exaggerated and spreading.

variables.name: Feeling a pinprick on the foot
variables.why: Every ascending tract is cut at T6, so signals from the foot cannot reach the cortex, even though they still drive the reflex.

why.correct: Golgi tendon organs sense tension. Their sensory neurons excite inhibitory interneurons that inhibit the motor neurons of the same muscle: the tendon reflex. The biceps' force drops, and the triceps is excited.
options: Direct excitation of the same muscle is what muscle spindles do in the stretch reflex. Tendon organs have the opposite effect.
Correct. The tendon reflex damps the tension in the muscle.
Tendon organ signals do reach the brain, but they also drive the spinal tendon reflex.
Crossing to the opposite limb is a feature of the crossed-extensor reflex, not of the tendon reflex.

why.correct: The triceps jerk runs mainly through C7. Because the other reflexes are normal, the problem is limited to that one segment or its root.
options: C5 carries the biceps jerk with C6, and the biceps jerk is normal.
Correct. C7 is the main segment for the triceps jerk.
L4 carries the knee jerk, which is normal.
S1 carries the ankle jerk, which is normal.

why.correct: Sensory: 0.6 ÷ 70 = 8.6 ms. Motor: 0.6 ÷ 30 = 20 ms. Add 1 ms for the synapse and 3 ms for the muscle: 8.6 + 20 + 1 + 3 = 32.6 ms, about 33 ms.
options: About 23 ms is the normal time, with the motor axons at 60 m/s. Halving their speed doubles the motor time.
About 13 ms would need faster, not slower, conduction.
Correct. The motor time doubles from 10 ms to 20 ms.
About 43 ms would need the sensory axons to slow down as well.

why.correct: Branches of the quadriceps spindle axons excite inhibitory interneurons, which release glycine onto the hamstring motor neurons and stop them firing. This is reciprocal inhibition.
options: Correct. Reciprocal inhibition through an inhibitory interneuron.
Straightening the knee does stretch the hamstrings, but stretching a muscle excites its own motor neurons. It does not relax it.
Tendon organs respond to tension, which rises only after the quadriceps contracts, and their main effect is on the quadriceps itself.
The reflex needs no signal from the brain, and it works when the tap comes as a surprise.

why.correct: This is the somatic motor neuron: a lower motor neuron whose myelinated axon runs from the ventral horn straight to skeletal muscle, the motor side of a somatic reflex.
options: Correct. One myelinated motor neuron from the cord to skeletal muscle.
A sensory neuron carries signals into the cord through the dorsal root. This axon leaves the cord toward a muscle.
An interneuron stays inside the CNS. This axon leaves the cord.
A ganglionic neuron sits in a ganglion outside the CNS and belongs to the two-neuron chain of a visceral reflex.

why.correct: The withdrawal reflex starts in nociceptors, runs through chains of interneurons that spread across several segments and across the midline, and so takes longer than the monosynaptic stretch reflex.
options: True. Harmful stimuli fire nociceptors; the stretch reflex starts in muscle spindles.
True. Lifting a limb needs flexors whose motor neurons lie in several segments.
False. It is polysynaptic. The stretch reflex is the monosynaptic one.
True. Extra synapses and slower pain axons lengthen the delay.
True. The crossed-extensor reflex straightens the other limb.

why.correct: Finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin, rapid alternating movements and walking test how accurately movements are coordinated, which is the cerebellum's job.
options: The mental status exam tests the cerebrum: consciousness, orientation, memory, language and judgment.
The sensory exam tests the ascending pathways and the sensory cortex.
The cranial nerve exam tests the brainstem and the nerves leaving it.
Correct. The coordination exam, with the gait exam, tests the cerebellum.

why.correct: Eyes open to pressure: E2. Sounds without words: V2. Bending away from pressure (normal flexion): M4. Total 2 + 2 + 4 = 8, in the severe range.
options: 6 would need a motor score of 2 (extension). Bending the arm away from pressure scores 4.
Correct. E2 + V2 + M4 = 8.
10 would need higher scores, for example eyes opening to voice and inappropriate words.
7 would need abnormal flexion (M3) rather than bending away from the pressure.

why.correct: Each category has a lowest score of 1, so a person with no responses at all scores 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. Full scores are 4 + 5 + 6 = 15.
options: No category scores 0; the lowest in each is 1.
Correct. From 3 (no response) to 15 (fully awake).
The maximum is 15, not 10, and the minimum is 3.
The minimum is 3 and the maximum is 15.

why.correct: This is a positive Romberg test. Loss of position and vibration sense means the dorsal column pathway, or the sensory axons feeding it, is damaged. With eyes open, vision makes up for the missing position sense; with eyes closed it cannot.
options: Cerebellar damage makes a person unsteady with the eyes open as well, and it does not remove vibration or position sense.
Correct. Lost position sense, compensated by vision, is the Romberg pattern.
Damage to the corticospinal tracts causes weakness with brisk reflexes, not loss of vibration and position sense.
The spinothalamic tracts carry pain and temperature, not vibration or position sense.

why.correct: Loss of stereognosis with normal basic sensation points to the sensory association cortex of the parietal lobe, which turns raw touch into recognition. The right hand is represented in the left hemisphere.
options: Dorsal column damage would remove fine touch and position sense in the hand, and his basic sensation is normal.
Correct. Stereognosis depends on the opposite parietal cortex.
A nerve injury would reduce touch and pinprick in the area the nerve supplies.
The cerebellum coordinates movement. It does not identify objects by touch.

why.correct: Whole-face weakness including the forehead is a lower motor neuron sign of the left facial nerve or its nucleus, which lies in the pons. The corticospinal axons for the right body run past it and have not yet crossed. One lesion on the left side of the pons hits both. Face on one side, body on the other is the mark of a brainstem lesion.
options: A left hemisphere lesion would weaken the right body and the lower right face, sparing the forehead. It would not weaken the left face.
A right hemisphere lesion would weaken the left body, not the right.
Correct. The left facial nucleus and the uncrossed corticospinal axons sit side by side here.
A cervical cord lesion would not affect the face, and a right-sided cord lesion would weaken the right body but not the left face.

why.correct: The corneal reflex is an arc through the brainstem: the touch goes in on the trigeminal nerve (V), interneurons pass it to both facial nuclei, and both facial nerves (VII) close the eyes.
options: The stimulus: a light touch on the clear front surface of the eye.
The sensory receptor and sensory neuron: endings of the ophthalmic branch of V.
The sensory neuron enters the brainstem and ends in the trigeminal nucleus.
The integration center: interneurons connect to the facial nuclei of both sides, which is why both eyes blink.
The motor neurons: the facial nerves drive the orbicularis oculi, the muscle that closes the eye.
The effector responds: both eyes close.

why.correct: In the corneal reflex, the touch travels in on the trigeminal nerve (V) of the side touched, and the blink goes out on both facial nerves (VII). Touching either eye makes the right eye blink, so both trigeminal nerves carry the touch in. The left eye never blinks, so the signal is not getting out to it: the left facial nerve.
options: If the left trigeminal nerve were damaged, touching the left eye would make neither eye blink. Here the right eye blinks every time.
The right eye blinks every time, so the right facial nerve works.
Correct. The motor side of the arc to the left eye has failed, so the left eye cannot close whichever eye is touched.
Touching the right eye still triggers a blink, so the right trigeminal nerve carries the touch in.

why.correct: Grade 3 is movement against gravity but not against resistance.
options: Grade 1 is a flicker of contraction with no movement.
Grade 2 is movement only with gravity taken away, such as sliding the arm along the bed.
Correct. Against gravity, not against resistance.
Grade 4 is movement against some resistance, which he cannot manage.

why.correct: This is pronator drift. Upper motor neuron damage weakens the arm's supinators and extensors more than its pronators and flexors, so the forearm turns palm-down and the arm sinks once vision stops correcting it.
options: Correct. Pronator drift is a sensitive sign of mild upper motor neuron weakness.
Cerebellar damage can make an arm wander or bounce, but turning palm-down and sinking is the classic sign of mild upper motor neuron weakness.
Holding a posture depends on strength and position sense, not on pain sensation.
A healthy person holds the position with the eyes closed.

why.correct: Ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes can look the same at the bedside, and a clot-dissolving drug would worsen bleeding. A scan must tell them apart first, as fast as possible.
options: Correct. Only a scan can tell a blocked artery from a burst one.
Waiting wastes the hours in which clot-dissolving treatment works. Nearly two million neurons can die each minute in a large stroke.
Her language problem is already clear from the history. A detailed exam would delay treatment and would not tell bleeding from blockage.
A lumbar puncture does not tell an ischemic stroke from a bleed into the brain, and it would delay treatment.

why.correct: BE FAST stands for balance, eyes, face, arm, speech and time. The signs of a stroke start suddenly.
options: Yes. Sudden loss of balance or coordination is the B.
Yes. Face droop is the F.
Yes. Arm weakness is the A.
No. A stroke starts suddenly. Memory loss that creeps in over months points to a slowly progressing disease.
Yes. Speech trouble is the S.

why.correct: Brief stroke-like signs that clear, with no dead tissue on the scan, define a transient ischemic attack. It is a warning: the risk of a full stroke is highest in the following days, so it is investigated and treated urgently.
options: Treating it as harmless misses the warning. Sudden one-sided weakness is assumed to be vascular until proven otherwise.
A stroke leaves dead brain tissue on the scan. His scan shows none.
Correct. A TIA, which needs urgent treatment.
Bleeding into the brain leaves blood and damaged tissue on the scan, and it does not clear in 20 minutes.

why.correct: The phrenic nerves to the diaphragm come from C3, C4 and C5. An injury at C4 can cut the descending drive to the phrenic motor neurons and destroy some of them, so the diaphragm may fail.
options: Swallowing is driven by cranial nerves from the brainstem, above the injury.
Correct. "C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive."
Eye movements are driven by cranial nerves III, IV and VI from the brainstem, above the injury.
Hearing travels in cranial nerve VIII to the brainstem, above the injury.

why.correct: Paraplegia is paralysis of the legs, from an injury in the thoracic cord or below. Tetraplegia (quadriplegia) is paralysis of all four limbs, from a cervical injury.
options: Weakness of one side of the body is called hemiplegia. Both paraplegia and tetraplegia affect both sides.
Correct. Legs only versus all four limbs.
The words describe which limbs are affected, not how long it lasts. Both can be complete or incomplete.
Both usually follow spinal cord damage. The level decides which one results.

why.correct: A hemisection (Brown-Séquard syndrome) removes the tracts that have already crossed (corticospinal) or have not yet crossed (dorsal columns) on the same side, and the spinothalamic tract carrying pain from the opposite side.

variables.name: Strength of the left leg
variables.why: The left lateral corticospinal tract, already crossed in the medulla, carries commands for the left leg.

variables.name: Knee jerk on the left
variables.why: The left leg's reflex arcs survive below the cut but lose descending control, so after an early absent phase they become brisk.

variables.name: Position sense in the left foot
variables.why: The left dorsal column carries position sense from the left side and does not cross until the medulla.

variables.name: Pain sensation in the right foot
variables.why: Pain from the right foot crosses within a segment or two of entry and climbs in the left spinothalamic tract, which is cut.

variables.name: Pain sensation in the left foot
variables.why: Pain from the left foot crosses to the right spinothalamic tract, which is intact.

variables.name: Strength of the arms
variables.why: The motor neurons and tracts for the arms are in the cervical cord, above T8.

why.correct: A complete C6 injury causes tetraplegia: the hands, trunk and legs lose their descending control, while the diaphragm (C3 to C5) and shoulder shrug (XI) are spared. In the first days, reflexes below the injury are absent; they return and become brisk over the following weeks.

variables.name: Voluntary movement of the legs
variables.why: Every descending motor tract passes through C6 on its way to the lumbar cord, and all are cut.

variables.name: Knee jerks
variables.why: Right after a sudden cord injury, the cord below goes quiet for days to weeks, and the reflexes are absent. They return and become brisk later.

variables.name: Movement of the diaphragm
variables.why: The phrenic motor neurons at C3 to C5 lie above the injury and keep their descending drive.

variables.name: Strength of the hand muscles
variables.why: The hand muscles are driven from C8 and T1, below the injury.

variables.name: Ability to shrug the shoulders
variables.why: Shrugging uses the accessory nerve (XI), whose motor neurons lie in the upper cervical cord, above the injury.

why.correct: The pinned region is the cerebellum, and the coordination exam, with the gait exam, tests it.
options: Correct. The coordination exam tests the cerebellum.
The mental status exam tests the cerebral cortex, not the cerebellum.
The sensory exam tests the ascending pathways in the spinal cord and brain.
The cranial nerve exam tests the nerves leaving the brain and brainstem.

why.correct: Weakness of the calf, a lost ankle jerk and numbness in the S1 dermatome all belong to one root on one side: lower motor neuron and sensory findings in the territory of left S1, often from a herniated disc.
options: Correct. Motor, reflex and sensory findings all fit one root.
Cortex damage would cause upper motor neuron signs: brisk reflexes and a Babinski sign, not a lost ankle jerk.
A cord lesion at T12 would affect both legs or produce upper motor neuron signs below it, not a single lost reflex with a dermatome of numbness.
Cerebellar damage causes clumsiness with normal strength and does not remove reflexes or sensation.

why.correct: A positive Romberg test, steady with eyes open and falling with eyes closed, tests position sense carried by the dorsal columns. A person with cerebellar damage is unsteady even with the eyes open.
options: Right pairing. Orientation, memory, language and judgment are cerebral functions.
Right pairing. The cranial nerves join the brain and brainstem at known levels.
This is the error. The Romberg test checks position sense, not the cerebellum.
Right pairing. Naming an object by touch needs the parietal cortex.
Right pairing. Reflexes test each arc and, through their briskness, the upper motor neuron control above it.

why.correct: Effortful, halting speech with good comprehension is expressive aphasia, found on the language part of the mental status exam. It points to Broca's area, in the left frontal lobe in most people.
options: Memory testing checks recall of new information, not the fluency of speech.
Damage to Wernicke's area causes fluent speech with poor comprehension, the opposite pattern.
Orientation tests whether a person knows who and where they are and the date, not how fluently they speak.
Correct. Expressive aphasia from Broca's area.
